technique.how: Hold the patient's head with both hands, ask them to fix on your nose, then deliver a small (10-20 degree) rapid, unpredictable head turn toward one side and watch the eyes at the end of the movement; repeat several times each side. A catch-up (corrective) saccade back to your nose after rotation toward one side indicates a deficient vestibulo-ocular reflex on that side.
technique.prerequisites: Only meaningful in acute vestibular syndrome (continuous vertigo with spontaneous nystagmus); patient alert, able to fixate, with adequate vision and neck mobility.
technique.contraindications: Cervical spine injury or instability, severe cervical stenosis, vertebral artery dissection concern; do not force a painful neck.

interpretation.positive_finding: A visible corrective saccade (abnormal HIT) points to a peripheral lesion (vestibular neuritis) on the side of head rotation and was present in all 25 peripheral AVS cases in the HINTS cohort.
interpretation.negative_finding: A normal head impulse (no corrective saccade) in a patient with acute spontaneous nystagmus is the single most worrying sign for stroke; it was found in 93% of central AVS and no peripheral cases.
interpretation.pitfalls: AICA-territory strokes can produce an abnormal HIT by infarcting the labyrinth or vestibular nerve entry zone, so a corrective saccade does not by itself exclude stroke. Small or slow impulses, covert saccades, and poor fixation make the test falsely normal; do not apply to patients without nystagmus.
interpretation.changes_what: Normal HIT in AVS: MRI and stroke pathway regardless of other findings. Abnormal HIT: supports neuritis only if nystagmus is unidirectional, no skew, and patient can walk.

estimates.target_condition: Central cause of acute vestibular syndrome; finding = normal (or untestable) horizontal head impulse test
estimates.population: 101 consecutive AVS patients with >=1 stroke risk factor (25 peripheral, 76 central), examined by neurologists/neuro-ophthalmologist
estimates.reference_standard: MRI (DWI) or CT plus clinical follow-up; peripheral lesions required normal MRI
estimates.computed_from: Table 1 proportions: h-HIT normal or untestable in 0% of 25 peripheral and 93% of 76 central AVS (includes 4 untestable); sensitivity 0.93, specificity 1.00; NLR 0.07 (0.03-0.15) as reported. LR+ undefined (no peripheral case had a normal HIT). Prevalence 76/101.
estimates.location: Table 1 (Key clinical features in patients with peripheral versus central AVS), PMC4593511

sources.citation: Kattah JC, Talkad AV, Wang DZ, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome: three-step bedside oculomotor examination more sensitive than early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging. Stroke. 2009;40(11):3504-3510.

Tarnutzer AA, Berkowitz AL, Robinson KA, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. Does my dizzy patient have a stroke? A systematic review of bedside diagnosis in acute vestibular syndrome. CMAJ. 2011;183(9):E571-E592.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Not valid outside acute vestibular syndrome (no spontaneous nystagmus, episodic or positional vertigo) or in patients who cannot fixate; results by non-expert examiners are substantially less accurate.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: A normal head impulse in a patient with continuous vertigo and nystagmus is a stroke sign; do not discharge on a peripheral diagnosis, obtain MRI (early DWI can be falsely negative in 12%).
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Estimates derive from expert bedside examination in a single high-risk cohort; HINTS meta-analysis of frontline clinicians (Ohle 2020, PMID 32167642) shows much lower specificity outside expert hands, and the 2009 cohort included 4 untestable HITs counted as dangerous.

extraction_notes: Sensitivity/specificity derived from the Table 1 row for 'h-HIT normal or untestable' in Kattah 2009 PMC full text (0% peripheral vs 93% central); Table 2 gives 62/69 ischemic strokes with normal HIT excluding untestable cases. LR+ left null because no peripheral patient had a normal HIT. Tarnutzer 2011 CMAJ pooled HIT figures not accessible (PMC abstract-only deposit), cited as context only.
